name: Methyl-1-testosterone (M1T)

lead: Methyl-1-testosterone (M1T) is an orally active synthetic androgen, the 17-alpha-methyl derivative of 1-testosterone. It appeared in early-2000s over-the-counter supplements aimed at bodybuilders chasing muscle growth and a bigger physique. It was never marketed for medical use.

It is an androgen receptor agonist, and a 2011 study identified it in a supplement and tested receptor affinity and anabolic and androgenic potency in animal and in vitro models. Research is limited to that animal and in vitro work, analytical papers and a case report.

paras: It was sold in supplements in the 2000s without medical approval; it is oral.
A case report describes acute kidney injury after combining it with ciclosporin. It is on the WADA prohibited list.

angle.text: It activates the androgen receptor, the route to more muscle growth and a bigger physique, and it was sold in early-2000s supplements for that purpose. Published material is animal work and a kidney-injury case report; the muscle-building use is anecdotal.

lead: Methyl-1-testosterone (M1T, SC-11195) is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid, the 17-alpha-methyl derivative of 1-testosterone. It was never marketed for medical use.[1] It appeared in the early 2000s in over-the-counter supplements aimed at bodybuilders.[2]

A 2011 study identified M1T in a supplement and examined it in animal and in vitro models; a published case report links it to kidney injury through an interaction with ciclosporin.[3][4] The World Anti-Doping Agency lists it as prohibited.[1]

paras: The 2011 characterisation study tested affinity for the androgen receptor in a yeast assay and tissue-specific androgenic and anabolic potency and side effects in animals, and examined metabolism.[3] Grokipedia (AI-generated) reports high receptor affinity, dose-dependent growth of levator ani muscle and prostate in rats, and effects on IGF-I expression.[2]

No studies found of M1T given to people in a trial. Human evidence consists of a case report of acute kidney injury in a patient with severe atopic dermatitis taking ciclosporin who had bought M1T online.[4] Analytical studies describe detection in urine and a supplement analysis.[5]

The case report authors advise physicians to ask about supplements bought online.[4] Grokipedia states that Health Canada issued warnings about supplements containing it and lists hepatotoxicity concerns for 17-alpha-alkylated steroids; it also reports WADA prohibition.[2]

timeline.event: Added to prohibited doping lists, according to a Chinese urine-monitoring study.[5]
